extracted.intended_audience: writers who give or receive feedback (Scribophile users and workshop participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for composing useful, actionable critiques of other writers' work in online workshops and critique groups; covers mindset, tone, scope (line edits vs critiques), consideration of authorial intent, and how to leverage critique groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be constructive / have best intentions
rubrics_metrics.description: Being constructive means coming to the critique with the ultimate goal of helping the writer improve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive criticism aims to help the writer, not to coddle or to browbeat. Be honest where necessary; refusing to offer valid criticism is a disservice. Deliver hard truths with genuine interest in the writer’s improvement. Anti-patterns: withholding needed criticism out of false kindness; offering empty praise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be genuine
rubrics_metrics.description: Approach criticism with sincere motivations and a desire to be helpful; genuineness leads to constructive commentary regardless of reviewer experience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your criticism is built on genuinely wanting to help, it will be constructive even if your technical skill is limited. Be honest about limits (e.g., genre knowledge) but keep the intention to improve the piece. Example: qualifying statements like 'I’m not familiar with this genre' are acceptable when genuine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tone — no jerks / be respectful
rubrics_metrics.description: Express hard truths without being rude or malicious; avoid unnecessarily harsh or obnoxious delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rude delivery causes authors to shut down and ignore valid points. Explain why something doesn’t work rather than berating. Anti-pattern: berating a phrase without explaining why it fails (author may dismiss even valid critique). Aim to communicate you have the author's best interest in mind.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t be too timid — offer necessary criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid depthless praise; do not withhold criticism out of fear of discouraging the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Praise when deserved, but if problems exist, point them out honestly. Even messy pieces often contain strengths—identify those too. Anti-pattern: 'flattering friends corrupt' — excessive, non-specific praise that provides no actionable feedback.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider authorial intent / context is king
rubrics_metrics.description: Try to understand what the author intended to communicate and judge the work on its own terms rather than imposing your own interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between 'This is how I’m hearing this' and 'This is what your words mean.' Ask whether the piece reaches its intended audience and accomplishes the author’s purpose. Anti-pattern: telling an author what their work 'is supposed to mean' without checking intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Call out the unintended or unspoken
rubrics_metrics.description: Flag places where meaning seems unclear, missing, or unintentionally implied.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask questions like 'Is that really what you meant?' Point out characters or plot elements that 'fall off the radar' or ambiguous wording. Tell the author when something reads as possibly unintended. Example: neologisms or unusual usage should be checked for intended meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for genre and intended audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate a piece in light of its genre conventions and the audience the author is targeting, not solely by your personal tastes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the story, plot devices, characters, and language are appropriate for the intended audience. If you dislike the genre, still assess competency within genre norms. Anti-pattern: harshly judging a romance because you dislike romance as a personal preference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t pretend to be a non-writer — bring your writerly insight
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are a writer, use both your gut reactions and your craft knowledge to explain why something works or doesn’t.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide higher-order craft observations (characterization, structure, pacing) in addition to reader reactions. Non-writers’ gut reactions are valuable too; best critiques combine both perspectives. Example: explain concrete reasons behind a reaction rather than only emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use your domain knowledge / 'critique what you know'
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage your life experience and any field-specific expertise to judge authenticity and factual accuracy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Experience in a specific field (e.g., a fry cook evaluating kitchen scenes) gives you authority to comment on authenticity even if your grammar isn’t perfect. Guidance: point out authentic vs. inauthentic portrayals; flag factual errors that undermine credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read widely and across media to improve critiquing
rubrics_metrics.description: Immerse yourself in many storytelling forms (books, movies, TV, etc.) to learn dialogue, plot, characterization and other storytelling techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exposure to great stories improves your intuitive sense of what works. Seek out exemplary works to learn patterns you can later identify and articulate in critiques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Learn from helpful critiques and iterate
rubrics_metrics.description: Study critiques that helped you and adapt their useful features into your own critiques; solicit feedback on your critiques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reread critiques that helped you understand why they worked. Ask authors how your critiques could be more helpful. Critiquing is a skill that improves with reflection and practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish line edits from critiques
rubrics_metrics.description: Line edits are detailed, line-by-line corrections of grammar/syntax; critiques address higher-level elements like characterization, plot, theme, scene structure, and language poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you want technical copyediting, request a line edit; if you want story-level feedback, request a critique. Line edits require strong grammar/syntax knowledge. Use Scribophile's inline critique options accordingly. Anti-pattern: expecting deep story critique from a manuscript that is still cluttered with distracting technical errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make your text readable to receive deep critique
rubrics_metrics.description: Deep, story-level criticism presupposes a readable manuscript that is generally free of distracting technical errors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Messy prose prevents readers from engaging with larger craft issues. If your prose is unreadable, ask for line edits first. Readers can’t resonate with story until technical hurdles are removed. That said, competent critics should still try to find gems in imperfect pieces.

rubrics_metrics.name: If seeking specific feedback, ask specific questions
rubrics_metrics.description: List at the top of your submission the sort of critique you’re seeking to focus reviewers' attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'I’d love to know how you reacted when X happened.' Specific prompts encourage readers to engage with particular aspects. This increases the chance you'll receive the feedback you need.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use critique groups effectively: contribute, be professional, build trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Leverage critique groups for broad exposure, multiple perspectives, and networking, but reciprocate and behave professionally to build long-term trade readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Benefits: (1) broad exposure to different demographics; (2) many eyes to catch recurring issues; (3) networking to find readers who will read long-form work. Rule of thumb: you get out what you put in. Anti-pattern: taking long reads without reciprocation or behaving unprofessionally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple readers strengthen diagnosis
rubrics_metrics.description: If several readers notice the same problem, it is likely a real issue with the text rather than individual taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use repeated observations as evidence of problem areas. Encourage a variety of readers to flag recurring issues early in revision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critiquing benefits your own writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewing other writers’ work helps you identify patterns and mistakes in your own writing and improves your craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As you spot what works and what doesn’t in others’ work, you can apply those lessons to your own drafts. Treat critique practice as a form of apprenticeship.
